title: Type Conversion and Casting
learningObjectives: Distinguish implicit conversions from explicit casts.
Explain integer promotions and the usual arithmetic conversions at a basic level.
Predict truncation when a floating value is converted to an integer type.
Recognize information loss and range problems in narrowing conversions.
Use explicit conversions only when their effects and valid ranges are understood.

understand.concept: C performs implicit conversions in assignments, arithmetic expressions, function calls and other contexts. An explicit cast requests a conversion to a specified type. Integer promotions and the usual arithmetic conversions determine the types used in many expressions. Conversions can change precision, signedness or range; an explicit cast does not make an otherwise unrepresentable value safe.
understand.whyItMatters: Conversion rules affect calculations, comparisons, function arguments and stored values. Explicitly understanding the resulting type prevents subtle truncation, signedness and precision defects.
understand.analogy: Think of a type as a contract that describes what kind of value an object can hold and which operations make sense for it.
understand.analogyLimit: The analogy is only an introduction; C types also determine representation, conversions, alignment and constraints.

explain.narrative:
## 1. Implicit conversion

When values of different arithmetic types are combined, C applies integer promotions and the usual arithmetic conversions. Assignment can also convert the right-hand value to the destination type. These rules affect both the intermediate calculation and the stored result.

## 2. Explicit casts

A cast such as `(double)count` converts count to double before the surrounding operation. This is useful when integer division would otherwise discard the fractional part. A cast should explain intent, not hide a type mismatch.

## 3. Integer division and truncation

If both operands of `/` are integers, the result is integer division. Converting the result afterward does not restore a discarded fraction. Convert an operand before division when a floating result is intended.

## 4. Narrowing conversions

Converting a wider or floating type to a narrower type can lose information. A floating-to-integer conversion discards the fractional part toward zero when the resulting integer is representable. Check range before converting values that may be out of range.

## 5. Follow the types through an expression

For every expression, identify operand types, promotions, common type and final destination type. Compiler warnings are useful, especially for signedness and narrowing conversions.

examples.title: Core example
examples.explanation: The cast converts whole to double before division, so the result retains the fractional part.

examples.title: A second case
examples.explanation: The explicit conversion to int discards the fractional part when the value is representable; it does not round to the nearest integer.

practise.guidedTask: Write a small C program that demonstrates the central rules in CL2.8. Compile with warnings enabled, run it with ordinary and boundary values, and explain each result in your own words.
practise.independentTask: Create a second example for CL2.8 using different values and names. Include one likely mistake as a separate experiment, observe the compiler diagnostic or behavior, then correct it. Record the rule that explains the correction.
hints: Start by identifying the exact type of every object and expression.
Check the C language rule before assuming a platform-specific result.
Use compiler warnings as feedback, not as proof of correctness.
Test normal values and important boundaries.
Explain why the result follows from the language rules.

questions.prompt: What is the result of `5 / 2` when both operands are int?
questions.explanation: Integer division discards the fractional part.
Casting an operand before division makes the arithmetic floating point.

questions.prompt: What does `(int)9.8` produce when the value is representable?
questions.explanation: Conversion from floating point to integer discards the fractional part toward zero.

questions.prompt: Does an explicit cast guarantee that a value is representable in the destination type?
options: No; range and information loss still need to be considered
Only casts to int are safe
questions.answer: No; range and information loss still need to be considered
questions.explanation: A cast requests a conversion but does not validate the source value.

questions.prompt: Why can assigning a large unsigned value to a smaller integer type be dangerous?
options: The destination may not represent the original value
The compiler converts it to a string
questions.answer: The destination may not represent the original value
questions.explanation: Narrowing conversions can lose information or have implementation-specific consequences.
